title: wb deletion audit
lede: Before the wb task-store layer moves to Go, each feature below gets one decision from you: keep it, tweak it, or delete it. Your choices save as you click. When you are done, press Copy answers and paste the result into chat.

stages.name: Sessions, tmux and PR data on the live page

decided.title: wb done opens the task file for review
decided.decision: No by default. By default wb done doesn't open anything, it just closes. The buffer becomes opt-in through a flag, proposed as wb done --review.

items.title: Gitignored-file sweep at wb done
items.question: What should wb done do with the gitignored files in a worktree before it deletes the worktree?
items.short_q: What happens to gitignored files at wb done?
items.why_it_matters: git worktree remove --force deletes gitignored files with no warning. Logs, scratch notes and repro data often live only there, so a wrong answer means silent data loss with no way back.
items.today: Before deleting the worktree, wb done lists the gitignored files in it as - [ ] keep lines. The ones you tick are copied into the task's dossier.
items.evidence_summary: It has saved real work once (logs and session data for be--monorepo--su-4696); most ignored files today are regenerable or bootstrap copies.
items.evidence_full: It has saved real work once: the kernel, supervisor and rabbit logs plus session data for be--monorepo--su-4696, now in that task's dossier. In today's worktrees the ignored files are mostly regenerable or bootstrap copies, such as config.hjson, node_modules and test outputs. The valuable minority is logs/, scratch/, investigate.json and session-data_*. It needs grep -oP and realpath -m, which fail on macOS, and one run stranded a ## Sweep section in a task file.
items.shift: The first pass said delete, because only 1 of 120 done tasks kept a file. The value pass says keep it with a tweak: deleting it means silent data loss with no way back, and the one save it made was a whole investigation's evidence.
items.recommendation: Make it automatic, with an allowlist: deleting would mean silent data loss, and keeping the interactive list conflicts with your decision that wb done doesn't open by default.

options.name: Make it automatic, with an allowlist
options.changes: Copy logs/, scratch/, *.md, *.json, *.log and session-data_* into the dossier, skipping anything credential-shaped and anything over a size cap. Print what was kept and what was skipped. The interactive tick list runs only under --review. No buffer and no task-file writes by default.
options.pros: Logs, scratch and session data survive without a tick list, and nothing opens by default.
options.trade: The interactive tick list moves behind --review.

options.name: Print only, copy nothing by default
options.changes: List the ignored files so you can see what is about to go. Copying happens only under --review.
options.pros: You can see what is about to go. Cheaper.
options.cost: A forgotten log is still lost.
options.trade: Cheaper, but nothing is saved unless you run with --review.

options.name: Keep as it is
options.risk: Conflicts with your decision that wb done doesn't open by default.

options.name: Delete
options.changes: Gitignored files die with the worktree.
options.pros: Removes a step that needs grep -oP and realpath -m, which fail on macOS.
options.cost: Gitignored files die with the worktree.
options.risk: Silent data loss with no way back.

options.name: Defer
options.changes: Decide when wb done moves to Go.
options.trade: Decide when wb done moves to Go.

items.title: Lock orphan auto-clear
items.question: Should wb keep its orphan-detection layer that sits on top of the per-task lock (the lock that stops two wb processes writing the same task at once)?
items.short_q: Keep the orphan-detection layer on the task lock?
items.why_it_matters: The layer exists for fear of a crashed lock holder leaving a task wedged, but that case never reaches it. It is the hardest-to-port code in wb, the only /proc use plus a date -d, and the task-store layer is moving to Go.
items.today: When a lock is contended, it checks whether the holder is an orphan, and if so tries to take the lock once more. It came from the July concurrency-safety plan.
items.today_full: It decides the holder is an orphan when it is alive, wb-shaped according to /proc/<pid>/cmdline, held for more than 60 s, and its tmux session gone. If so, it tries to take the lock once more. (Corrected 2026-10-18: it never deletes the lock or stops the holder, so that second try only succeeds if the lock was freed in the meantime.)
items.evidence_summary: It has never fired in 60 days of transcripts. About 125 lines plus about 90 test lines.
items.evidence_full: It has never fired. Every contention message in 60 days of transcripts is a test fixture. A crashed holder never reaches this code, because the kernel releases a flock when its process dies, and a separate kill -0 retry already covers that case. The only case it handles is a holder that is alive but stuck, and there a loud exit naming the holder is acceptable. It is the only /proc use in wb, plus a date -d. About 125 lines, plus about 90 test lines.
items.recommendation: Delete the orphan layer: it has never fired, the crashed-holder case is already covered without it, and it is the hardest code to port.

options.name: Delete the orphan layer; keep the plain lock and the dead-pid retry
options.changes: Removes the orphan layer. The lock itself stays, because it fixed a real lost write.
options.pros: Removes the hardest-to-port code: about 125 lines plus about 90 test lines, and the only /proc use.
options.cost: A holder that is alive but stuck gets a loud exit naming it, which is judged acceptable.
options.trade: The plain lock and the dead-pid retry stay.

options.name: Shrink to a message only
options.changes: On contention, print the holder plus a 'probably orphaned' hint, and never auto-clear.
options.trade: Never auto-clears; only prints the holder and a hint.

options.name: Keep and port
options.changes: The layer stays and gets ported to Go.
options.cost: Go would need a portable replacement for the /proc check, such as ps.

items.title: wb sync
items.question: Should wb sync, the command that fetches the task store and fast-forward merges it, be deleted?
items.why_it_matters: It was added so that no agent reaches for git reset --hard. The pre-tool-use guard's refusal message names it, so deleting it means the guard's text must change in the same commit.
items.today: A safe way to pull the store's GitHub remote: it fetches the task store and fast-forward merges it. Nothing runs it automatically.
items.evidence_summary: No real runs, apart from about 8 in one be--monorepo spike.
items.evidence_full: No real runs, apart from about 8 in one be--monorepo spike. Nothing runs it automatically. The Mac decision says each machine has its own store and they never sync, so the only other writer is this same machine. The pre-tool-use guard's refusal message names it. It's about 100 portable lines plus a 222-line test.
items.recommendation: Delete it: it has had no real use, and with one store per machine nothing else writes to the store. Confidence is medium-low.

options.name: Delete; guard text says git -C ~/code/tasks pull --ff-only
options.changes: Edit the guard message, the guards guide and the wb-guide row in the same change.
options.pros: Removes about 100 portable lines plus a 222-line test.
options.cost: The guard message, the guards guide and the wb-guide row must change in the same change.
options.trade: The guard text points at git -C ~/code/tasks pull --ff-only instead.

options.name: Keep
options.trade: Its value is mostly as the guard's suggested alternative.

items.title: "(auto)" stamps in ## Handoffs
items.question: Which of the (auto) stamps that wb verbs write into a task's ## Handoffs should we keep?
items.why_it_matters: /wb-resume uses the stamps to notice that something happened after the last /wb-save, and then asks before picking up the old plan. Drop the wrong ones and that check stops working.
items.today: wb verbs append ### <time> — <verb> (auto) plus one line to the task's Handoffs.
items.evidence_summary: 368 stamps in 215 files. wb-resume only checks whether any stamp exists after the last save; it never reads what they say.
items.evidence_full: 368 stamps in 215 files: resume 111, done 98, set 95, status 30, down 25, breakdown 8. wb-resume only checks whether any stamp exists after the last save; it never reads what they say. The set and status stamps (125) repeat what the frontmatter already shows, and git history on the store records the change anyway.

prior.note: I need more context: what actually reads these stamps, and what breaks if they go?
prior.reply: Only /wb-resume reads them, and only to ask: is there any stamp after the last /wb-save? It never reads their text. Dropping the set/status stamps keeps that check working because resume/down/pause/done/breakdown still stamp. Dropping all of them means wb-resume must compare against the store git log instead.

items.recommendation: Drop the set and status stamps and keep the lifecycle ones: the 125 set and status stamps repeat the frontmatter, and the lifecycle stamps keep wb-resume's gap check working.

options.name: Drop the set and status stamps; keep the lifecycle ones
options.changes: Resume, down, pause, done and breakdown keep stamping, so wb-resume's gap check keeps working.
options.pros: A field change no longer rewrites the body, and wb-resume's gap check keeps working.

options.name: Drop all stamps
options.changes: wb-resume compares the last save against the store's git log or file mtime instead.
options.cost: A change to the wb-resume skill.
options.trade: wb-resume compares against the store's git log or file mtime instead of stamps.
